source_text:
Daemonum eam esse naturam, ut aerii corporis sensu terrenorum corporum sensum facile praecedant, celeritate etiam propter eiusdem aerii corporis superiorem mobilitatem non solum cursus quorumlibet hominum uel ferarum, uerum etiam uolatus auium inconparabiliter uincant. quibus duabus rebus, quantum ad aerium corpus attinet, praediti, hoc est acrimonia sensus et celeritate motus, multo ante cognita praenuntiant uel nuntiant, quae homines pro sensus terreni tarditate mirentur. accessit etiam daemonibus per tam longum tempus. quo eorum uita protenditur, rerum longe maior experientia, quam potest hominibus propter breuitatem uitae prouenire. per has efficacias, quas aerii corporis natura sortita est, non solum multa futura praedicunt daemones, uerum etiam multa mira faciunt. quae quoniam homines dicere ac facere non possunt, eos dignos quidam, quibus seruiant et quibus diuinos honores deferant, arbitrantur instigante maxime uitio curiositatis propter amorem felicitatis falsae atque terrenae excellentiae temporalis. qui autem se ab his cupiditatibus mundant nec eis se ferendos rapiendosque permittunt, sed inquirunt et amant aliquid, quod eodem modo semper est, cuius participatione beati sint, primum considerant non ideo sibi praeponendos esse daemones, quod acriore sensu corporis praeualent. aerii scilicet, hoc est subtilioris elementi, quia nec in ipsis terrenis corporibus bestias sibi praeponendas putant, quae acrius multa praesentiunt; uelut sagacem canem, quia latentem feram olfactu acerrimo sic inuenit, ut ad eam capiendam ducatum quendam homini praebeat, non utique prudentiore intellectu animi, sed acutiore corporis sensu; uel uulturem. quia proiecto cadauere ex inprouisa longinquitate aduolat: nec aquilam, quia sublimiter uolans de tanto interuallo natantem sub fluctibus piscem dicitur peruidere et grauiter aquis inlisa exertis pedibus atque unguibus rapere; nec alia multa animantium genera, quae inter herbas saluti suae noxias pascendo circumerrant nec aliquid earum, quo laedantur, adtingunt, cum eas homo uix experiendo cauere didicerit et multa innoxia, quod sint inexperta, formidet. unde conicere facile est, quanto possit in aeriis corporibus sensus esse acrior. nec ideo tamen daemones, qui eo praediti sunt, bonis hominibus praeponendos prudens quisque censuerit. hoc et de corporum celeritate dixerim. et hac enim praestantia non solum a uolucribus homines, uerum etiam a multis quadrupedibus ita superantur, ut in eorum conparatione plumbei deputandi sint; nec tamen ideo sibi haec animantium genera existimant praeponenda, quibus capiendis, mansuefaciendis atque in suae uoluntatis usum commodumque redigendis non ui corporis, sed rationis imperant.
Illam uero tertiam daemonum potentiam, quod diuturna rerum experientia quemadmodum praenoscant atque praenuntient multa didicerunt, ita contemnunt, qui haec uigilanter curant a uerissimae lucis ueritate discernere, ut nec malos senes plura expertos et ob hoc quasi doctiores ideo probi adulescentes sibi antecellere existiment nec medicos nec nautas nec agricolas,, quos prauae uoluntatis et iniquis moribus uiderint, ideo putent sibi esse praeferendos, quod illi de ualitudinibus, illi de tempestatibus, illi de arbustorum fructuumque generibus multa ita praenuntiant, ut harum rerum inexperto diuinare uideantur.
thought_title: Demons' natural advantages do not make them superior
orientation: Augustine is now answering the question where divinations come from, and begins by granting that demons have a natural excellence of airy body, keen senses, speed, and long experience, but argues that none of this makes them worthy of worship or superior to good humans.
pass_a_gloss: That the nature of demons is such that by the sense of an airy body they easily surpass the sense of earthly bodies, and also by speed, because of the superior mobility of the same airy body, they incomparably surpass not only the running of any humans or wild beasts, but even the flight of birds. Endowed with these two things, as far as it pertains to the airy body, that is, keenness of sense and speed of movement, they announce or foretell things known far in advance, which humans, because of the slowness of earthly sense, wonder at. There has also come to demons through so long a time, for which their life is extended, a far greater experience of things than can come to humans because of the shortness of life. Through these efficacies, which the nature of the airy body has obtained, demons not only predict many future things, but also do many wonders. And because humans cannot say and do these things, certain people judge them worthy to be served and to have divine honors conferred on them, especially at the instigation of the vice of curiosity because of love of false happiness and of earthly, temporal excellence. But those who cleanse themselves from these desires and do not allow themselves to be carried away and seized by them, but seek and love something that is always in the same way, by participation in which they may be blessed, first consider that demons are not for this reason to be placed before them, because they prevail by keener sense of body, that is, of the airy, that is, of a more subtle element, because not even among earthly bodies themselves do they think beasts should be placed before them, which perceive many things more keenly; for example, a keen-scented dog, because it finds a hidden wild beast by its sharpest sense of smell so that it offers a kind of guidance to a human for catching it, not indeed by a wiser understanding of mind, but by a keener sense of body; or a vulture, because it flies to a corpse thrown out from unforeseen distance; nor an eagle, because flying high it is said to see through from so great an interval a fish swimming under the waves and to seize it, striking the waters heavily with feet and claws stretched out; nor many other kinds of living things, which wander about feeding among herbs harmful to their own safety and do not touch any of them by which they may be harmed, although a human has scarcely learned to avoid them by experience and fears many harmless things because they are untried. From this it is easy to infer how much keener sense can be in airy bodies. And yet no wise person would judge that demons, who are endowed with it, are for that reason to be placed before good humans. I would say this also about speed of bodies. For by this excellence too humans are surpassed not only by birds, but also by many four-footed animals, so much that in comparison with them they should be considered leaden; and yet they do not think these kinds of living things are for that reason to be placed before themselves, over which they rule not by force of body, but by the command of reason, for catching them, taming them, and reducing them to the use and convenience of their own will. But that third power of demons, that by long experience of things they have learned how they foreknow and foretell many things, those who vigilantly care to discern these things from the truth of the truest light so despise it, that they do not think that wicked old men, who have experienced more and for this reason are as it were more learned, therefore surpass good young men, nor do they think that physicians or sailors or farmers, whom they see to be of depraved will and unjust character, are for that reason to be preferred to themselves, because those foretell many things about states of health, those about storms, those about kinds of trees and fruits, so that to one inexperienced in these things they seem to divine.

choices.english: by the sense of an airy body
choices.why: Keeps the instrumental ablative force and the glossary term 'airy body' for aerium corpus.

choices.english: have divine honors conferred on them
choices.why: Uses the glossary rendering 'divine honors' and keeps the passive sense of deferant with dative of recipient.

choices.term: felicitatis falsae atque terrenae excellentiae temporalis
choices.english: of false happiness and of earthly, temporal excellence
choices.why: Preserves the two genitives as parallel objects of 'amorem' and keeps 'earthly' and 'temporal' as distinct adjectives modifying 'excellentiae'.
rejected: of false happiness and temporal earthly excellence
of a false blessedness and of earthly temporal preeminence

choices.why: Keeps the gerundive of obligation with 'deputare' as 'consider' and the literal 'leaden' for the metaphor of heaviness and slowness.
rejected: they must be reckoned as lead
they are to be counted as made of lead

choices.term: in suae uoluntatis usum commodumque redigendis
choices.english: reducing them to the use and convenience of their own will
choices.why: Keeps the gerundive purpose force and the double object 'usum commodumque' as 'use and convenience'.
rejected: bringing them into the service and advantage of their own will
subjecting them to their own will's use and benefit

choices.english: to discern these things from the truth of the truest light
choices.why: Keeps the ablative of separation with 'a' and the superlative 'uerissimae' as 'truest', preserving the theological contrast between demonic knowledge and divine truth.
rejected: to distinguish these from the truth of the most true light
to separate these things from the truth of the truest light

pass_b_english: The nature of demons is such that the sense of an airy body easily surpasses the sense of earthly bodies, and because of the superior mobility of that same airy body they incomparably outstrip in speed not only the running of any human beings or wild animals, but even the flight of birds. Endowed with these two things, as far as the airy body is concerned—keenness of sense and swiftness of movement—they foretell or announce things known long in advance, which human beings marvel at because of the slowness of earthly sense. Demons have also gained, through the very long time over which their life extends, a far greater experience of things than can come to human beings because of the brevity of life. Through these capacities, which the nature of an airy body has obtained, demons not only predict many future things, but also perform many wonders. Since human beings cannot say or do these things, some people judge the demons worthy to be served and to have divine honors conferred on them, urged on especially by the vice of curiosity because of the love of false happiness and of earthly, temporal excellence.

But those who cleanse themselves from these desires and do not allow themselves to be carried off and seized by them, but instead seek and love something that is always the same, by sharing in which they may be blessed—these people first consider that demons should not be placed above them because they prevail with a keener sense of body. That is, because they belong to an airy, that is, a subtler element. For they do not think that even among earthly bodies the beasts should be placed above them, though beasts perceive many things more keenly. Take the keen-scented dog: because it finds a hidden wild animal by its sharpest sense of smell and offers a kind of guidance to a human being for catching it, not by a wiser intellect of mind but by a keener sense of body. Or the vulture, because it flies to a corpse thrown out from an unforeseen distance. Nor the eagle, because flying high it is said to see from so great an interval a fish swimming beneath the waves and, striking the waters heavily, to seize it with outstretched feet and talons. Nor many other kinds of living creatures, which wander about among grasses harmful to their health while feeding and do not touch any of them by which they would be harmed, though a human being has scarcely learned to avoid them by experience and fears many harmless things because they are untested. From this it is easy to infer how much keener sense can be in airy bodies. Yet no prudent person would judge that demons, who are endowed with it, should therefore be placed above good human beings.

I would say the same about swiftness of body. In this excellence too human beings are so surpassed not only by birds but also by many four-footed animals that in comparison with them they should be considered leaden. Yet people do not think these kinds of living creatures should be placed above them, creatures whom they rule over—capturing them, taming them, and reducing them to the use and convenience of their own will—not by force of body but by reason.

As for that third power of demons, that by long experience of things they have learned how to know and foretell many things in advance—those who vigilantly take care to discern these things from the truth of the truest light despise it so much that they do not think wicked old men, who have experienced more and are therefore, so to speak, more learned, excel upright young people. Nor do they think physicians, sailors, or farmers whom they see to be of depraved will and unjust character should be preferred to themselves, because those men foretell many things about illnesses, those about storms, those about the kinds of trees and fruits, so that to someone inexperienced in these matters they seem to divine.

last_rejected.quote: they foretell or announce things known long in advance
last_rejected.source_quote: multo ante cognita praenuntiant uel nuntiant
last_rejected.why: "multo ante" modifies "cognita," not the verbs: things known long before, not known long in advance of foretelling.
last_rejected.fix: they foretell or announce things that were known long before
last_rejected.ruling: 'multo ante cognita' = known long before; 'known long in advance' conveys same meaning adequately.

last_rejected.quote: Through these capacities, which the nature of an airy body has obtained
last_rejected.source_quote: per has efficacias, quas aerii corporis natura sortita est
last_rejected.why: "sortita est" means has been endowed with/allotted, not obtained; nature possesses the capacities, not obtains them.
last_rejected.fix: Through these capacities, which the nature of an airy body has been endowed with
last_rejected.ruling: 'obtained' is within normal range for 'sortita est'; no meaning changed or lost.

last_rejected.quote: because they belong to an airy, that is, a subtler element
last_rejected.source_quote: aerii scilicet, hoc est subtilioris elementi
last_rejected.why: Ablative of quality/modification: "aerii...elementi" describes the body, not possession; demons are not said to "belong to" an element.
last_rejected.fix: that is, of an airy, that is, a subtler element
last_rejected.ruling: 'belong to an airy element' reasonably renders 'aerii elementi'; no misleading change.

last_rejected.why: "inprouisa" means unexpected/unforeseen modifying distance, but the Latin means the distance is unexpected to others, not that the vulture comes from somewhere unforeseen; better: from an unexpected distance.
last_rejected.ruling: 'unforeseen distance' and 'unexpected distance' are near-synonymous; no real error.

last_rejected.why: "grauiter" with "inlisa" means falling heavily into/sinking deep into the waters, not striking heavily; the eagle plunges down.
last_rejected.ruling: 'striking heavily' vs 'falling heavily' both within range for 'grauiter inlisa'; no major shift.

last_rejected.quote: these kinds of living creatures should be placed above them, creatures whom they rule over
last_rejected.source_quote: nec tamen ideo sibi haec animantium genera existimant praeponenda, quibus capiendis, mansuefaciendis atque in suae uoluntatis usum commodumque redigendis non ui corporis, sed rationis imperant
last_rejected.why: The relative clause explains why they are NOT preferred, not a concession: humans rule them by reason, hence humans are superior despite bodily inferiority.
last_rejected.fix: these kinds of living creatures should be placed above them, since over them—capturing, taming, and reducing them to use—humans rule not by bodily force but by reason
last_rejected.ruling: English correctly says creatures NOT preferred; relative clause adds context, not a concession error.

last_rejected.quote: those who vigilantly take care to discern these things from the truth of the truest light despise it so much
last_rejected.source_quote: qui haec uigilanter curant a uerissimae lucis ueritate discernere, ita contemnunt
last_rejected.why: "ita...ut" construction: they despise it TO SUCH A DEGREE that...; the result clause is broken in English, losing the correlative structure.
last_rejected.fix: those who vigilantly take care to discern these things from the truth of the truest light despise it to such a degree that
last_rejected.ruling: 'despise it so much that' preserves 'ita...ut'; result clause follows correctly.

last_rejected.quote: they do not think wicked old men, who have experienced more and are therefore, so to speak, more learned, excel upright young people
last_rejected.source_quote: ut nec malos senes plura expertos et ob hoc quasi doctiores ideo probi adulescentes sibi antecellere existiment
last_rejected.why: "ideo" goes with the main clause, not the old men: young people do not think old men excel them FOR THAT REASON (because of experience).
last_rejected.fix: they do not think that for that reason wicked old men, who have experienced more and are therefore, so to speak, more learned, excel upright young people
last_rejected.ruling: 'therefore' captures 'ideo' adequately; placement difference does not change meaning.
